title: The poorest
hook: the Guru's honor of the humble
tomorrow: smoke day: the sky goes orange. why would anyone call air a Guru?

segments.voice: Yesterday, water for both sides: Bhai Kanhaiya's water for anyone hurt, and the wrong still remembered. Today, a quieter kind of honor, and it smells like bread.
screen: `WATER FOR BOTH SIDES.` → `IT SMELLS LIKE BREAD.`

segments.voice: Six in the morning, and Arjan's apartment smells of roti on a hot pan. Simran is there early to walk him to the bus. His dad has just come in from a night shift at the car wash, hands red and cracked from the cold water, and he won't sit down until Simran has a plate. Plain roti, salt, a smear of ghee. She takes a bite, and it's the best thing she's eaten all week. Sikh tradition has a story about a meal like this, and a choice between two tables.
screen: `ROTI ON A HOT PAN.` → `HANDS CRACKED FROM A NIGHT SHIFT.` → `PLAIN BREAD, SALT, GHEE.` → `TWO TABLES.`

segments.voice: The janamsakhis, the old stories of Guru Nanak's life, tell it this way. In the town of Saidpur, the Guru stays with Bhai Lalo, a carpenter, and eats his coarse bread. A wealthy official, Malik Bhago, throws a feast and is offended when the Guru doesn't come. So the Guru takes Lalo's bread in one hand and Bhago's rich food in the other, and squeezes. From Lalo's, tradition says, milk runs out. From Bhago's, blood. Bread earned by honest work, and food squeezed out of other people's labor. The point isn't that money is bad. It's which table honors the people who did the work. Here's the detail worth telling a friend tonight: Lalo isn't only a story. Guru Nanak names him in a hymn on Ang 722, the same Lalo from the bus stop day. And on Ang 15, Guru Nanak puts it plainly, in paraphrase: Nanak stands with the lowest of the low; why would he compete with the great? Where the lowly are cared for, there your grace rains down. Kirat, honest work, is one of the things Sikh life stands on. So honoring the humble isn't pity. It's sitting at their table, taking the plate, and saying the bread is good, because it is. Simran asks for a second roti. Arjan's dad grins for the first time.
screen: `LALO'S BREAD, BHAGO'S FEAST.` · `MILK, AND BLOOD.` · `NANAK STANDS WITH THE LOWEST.` · `HONOR ISN'T PITY.` · then, large: `HONOR THE HUMBLE.`

segments.voice: If there's something plain to eat near you, bread, a cracker, a spoon of rice, hold it and smell it first. Eat it slowly, and think of the hands that grew it, ground it, cooked it and carried it, especially the ones paid least. Keep tasting until there's nothing left.
The poorest. The people Guru Nanak stood with: honored by sitting at their table and taking the bread, not by pity.
The line to keep: honor the humble, at their table, with thanks. A second roti before the bus on day 1733.

howItsDone: Sikhs tell the story of Bhai Lalo and Malik Bhago to honor kirat, honest work, and in the langar the food is shared at one level, whoever cooked it and whoever eats it.

myth: the Lalo story teaches that rich people can't be good
the point is which table honors the people who did the work: honest work versus food squeezed from others.
Bhai Lalo is named in a hymn of Guru Nanak
Ang 722. he isn't only a story character.
honoring the poor mostly means feeling sorry for them
honor isn't pity: Guru Nanak sat at Lalo's table and ate his bread.

fork.setup: at a fancy dinner, everyone at your table talks over the server and never looks up. going by today, what fits best?
options: look up, thank her by name if you can, and mean it.
leave a big tip so she knows someone noticed her.
say nothing; it's her job, and she's used to it.
fork.reveal: honor the humble isn't pity or payment: it's seeing the person and honoring the work, the way Guru Nanak sat at Lalo's table.

original.note: Gurmukhi: kirat, honest work, like Bhai Lalo's bread.

trapdoor: what you thought: helping the poor means giving them things from above.
what it means: honoring the humble by sitting at their table and honoring their work.
what a scholar hears: the janamsakhi story of Lalo and Malik Bhago at Saidpur; Lalo named in Tilang (Ang 722); 'neecha andar neech jaat... Nanak tin kai sang saath' (Ang 15, Sri Raag).
guess: the people Guru Nanak stood with, honored at their table
people who chose to give up all they had for God
anyone who can't afford to give to the gurdwara

chat.says: arjan's dad made me eat first, after a whole night shift. should i have said no?
options: no, say yes. Guru Nanak ate Lalo's bread; honor means taking the plate.
yes. he needs it more, and taking from a poor family is never okay.
eat it, but leave money under the plate so it's fair on both sides.
chat.meaning: Guru Nanak sat at Lalo's table and ate his coarse bread. Honoring the humble isn't pity or paying back: it's receiving, with thanks.

janamsakhis.meaning: old collections of stories about Guru Nanak's life

Saidpur.meaning: the town where tradition places the Lalo story

Malik Bhago.meaning: a wealthy official in the Lalo story

ghee.meaning: clarified butter, used in Punjabi cooking

kirat.meaning: honest work, earning by your own effort
